title: Does a Singapore company need a MAS licence to pay suppliers in RLUSD?
abstract: Sourced guide to when Singapore's Payment Services Act licensing applies to digital payment tokens, what MAS says about stablecoins, and the licence classes.
body:
According to the Monetary Authority of Singapore, merely accepting digital payment tokens does not by itself trigger a Payment Services Act licence. The test in its April 2024 FAQ is a clear intention to then transmit, or arrange the transmission of, the accepted tokens to another party as a service. [1]

The same FAQ says that entities that buy or sell digital payment tokens, or establish or operate a DPT exchange, are regulated, and that stablecoins may meet the definition of a digital payment token: it names USD Coin and Tether as examples, says MAS examines each stablecoin's characteristics, and does not mention RLUSD. [1]

According to MAS's overview of the Act, the licence classes are Standard Payment Institution and Major Payment Institution. A Standard Payment Institution is limited to payment transactions of S$3 million a month for one payment service and S$6 million a month for two or more; a Major Payment Institution has no such limit and must hold base capital of at least S$250,000. [2]

Author interpretation: a company that only pays its own suppliers from its own wallet looks like a user of a token rather than a provider of a payment service, but the FAQ gives no yes-or-no answer for that case and this is not legal advice. Licensing becomes a likelier question if the company moves tokens for other parties, runs an exchange or holds tokens for others. Confirm with Singapore counsel or MAS. Sources accessed 11 November 2026. [1][2]
